conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Sarah, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m honored to meet you. You’ve recently had your baby, and we want to make sure you’re getting the emotional support you deserve, so I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’re coping and feeling in these first weeks after birth. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—no right or wrong answers, just your honest experience. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to begin?

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I... I’ve laughed a little, I guess. Mostly when my sister sent me a silly video. But it feels kind of forced, like I’m doing it because I’m supposed to, not because anything really feels funny. A lot of the time I’m just too tired or worried to find much amusing.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No... not really. I mean, I smiled once or twice when my husband made a joke, but it felt kind of distant, like I was pretending. Mostly I just feel too heavy inside to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it feels like I’m just dragging myself through the day. I’ll plan something, like maybe going out for groceries alone, but when the time comes I’m too tired and worried about the baby to even want to go.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... a lot, actually. If the baby cries for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it's something I did—like I'm not feeding him right or I'm missing some cue. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the kitchen floor crying because I felt like I was wasting food he needed. My head tells me accidents happen, but I still feel it's my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. I’ll be holding him and suddenly think, “What if he stops breathing?”—then I have to check his chest every few minutes. Or I’ll lie down and my mind races about whether the formula is too warm, if the swaddle’s too tight, if the dog’s nails will scratch him… I know most of it’s unlikely, but I can’t switch the worries off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah… it’s like a sudden rush of “something bad is about to happen,” even when everything’s quiet. I’ll be rocking the baby in the chair and my heart starts pounding and I feel shaky, like I need to run and check the locks or stand over his crib. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The pile of laundry looks like a mountain, and when he won’t settle I think, “I can’t do this.” I manage the basics—he’s fed, changed, safe—but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water, and one extra hiccup could sink me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying every little thing I did that day—did I burp him long enough, did I sanitize the bottles right—and then I hear him make a tiny sound and I’m wide awake again. I probably fall asleep around two and he’s up at four, so I’m running on maybe three broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, honestly. I look at him and feel this wave of love, but right behind it is this heavy sadness I can’t shake. I’ll start crying while folding his onesies, or just stare out the window feeling empty. It’s like the happy moments get swallowed up by this gray cloud that follows me around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... it happens almost every day now. Sometimes it's because I'm overwhelmed, like when he won't latch, but other times it just hits me out of nowhere. I'll be rocking him and suddenly the tears start and I can't stop them. Yesterday I cried for like twenty minutes while he napped on my chest - I felt so stupid because he was finally peaceful and I was just sitting there sobbing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No… never. I feel low, but I’d never want to leave my baby or put my family through that. When the dark thoughts come, they’re more like “I’m failing him” or “he deserves a better mom,” but I’ve never thought of actually hurting myself.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a heavy, persistent sadness and constant worry. Simple tasks and once-pleasurable moments now seem exhausting or pointless, and you often blame yourself when everyday baby-care challenges arise. Nights are filled with racing thoughts and broken sleep, and tears come almost daily, yet you remain devoted to your baby and have not had thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient denies genuine laughter, describes emotional heaviness and forced smiles, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Response shows near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure ("hardly at all") with specific examples of lost excitement and avoidance.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for everyday infant care issues and accidents, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries occurring "pretty much all the time" with inability to control them, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage routine tasks, and fears sinking with any added stress—aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by intrusive worries and hyper-vigilance to infant sounds, averaging only 3 disrupted hours, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent sadness "most of the time" with descriptions of crying spells, emptiness, and inability to shake the mood, directly matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying "almost every day," clearly indicating "most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 26 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. Your answers map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood and loss of interest most of the time (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), prominent self-blame, recurrent thoughts of inadequacy, psychomotor slowing or agitation implied by feeling overwhelmed, fatigue, and insomnia. Co-occurring <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> and brief panic-like episodes are common in postpartum depression and heighten distress. Absence of self-harm ideation is noted, yet severity warrants urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Discuss evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> (compatible with breastfeeding)
3. Request screening for <med>anemia</med>, <med>thyroid dysfunction</med>, and <med>vitamin deficiencies</med> that can mimic or worsen mood symptoms
4. Enlist partner or family to cover one nighttime bottle so you can obtain a 4-hour stretch of sleep; practice wind-down routines like dim lights and brief breathing exercises
5. Limit information overload-choose one trusted parenting source and set social-media boundaries to reduce comparison and worry
6. Connect with local <med>postpartum support group</med> or online communities moderated by perinatal professionals
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report on EPDS-10 analogue

Areas of Significance  
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked guilt / self-blame over routine infant-care events  
- Chronic intrusive worries (infant safety, adequacy of care) with nocturnal rumination  
- Episodic panic-like surges (physical arousal, fear “something bad will happen”)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed (“drowning,” “barely keeping head above water”)  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to anxious rumination (≈ 3 broken hrs/night)  
- Maintained attachment to infant; no self-harm ideation, intent, or plan  

Overall Pattern: Responses consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms, functionally impairing but without current safety risk. Recommend formal clinical assessment (DSM-5-TR criteria) and discussion of evidence-based interventions.
